usage: Korean also uses 죽다 for batteries/phones going dead, just like English.
죽겠어요 after an adjective is a super common way to exaggerate a feeling, not literal.
examples: Plants and animals dying use 죽다 directly.
배고파 죽겠어요 is everyday spoken exaggeration.
Used when a phone battery runs out.
nuance: 죽다 is the plain word for dying, but in daily speech Koreans rarely say it literally about people. Far more often you hear '-아/어 죽겠어요' tacked onto a feeling (배고파 죽겠어요, 더워 죽겠어요) to mean 'so much I could die'. It also works for machines and batteries that stop working.
mistakes: Don't confuse 죽다 (to die) with 죽이다 (to kill) — adding 이 makes it 'cause to die'.

usage: 놀다 means 'hang out / spend fun time', not only child's play.
If you have time today, let's hang out
Casual 놀자 is how friends invite each other to meet up.
examples: I hang out with friends on the weekend
Common way to talk about weekend plans.
The kids are playing in the park
Children playing uses the same verb.
Shall we hang out at my place?
놀까요 suggests meeting up to relax together.
nuance: 놀다 covers both children 'playing' and adults 'hanging out / having fun together', so it is one of the most-used social verbs. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, ㅅ — hence 놉니다 and the polite command 노세요 (not 놀세요). Note: 놀다 carries a relaxed, fun feeling, so don't use it for serious meetings.
mistakes: Don't write the polite command as 놀으세요 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 노세요.

usage: 걸리다 with 시간 is THE way to ask about duration.
감기에 걸리다 = 'catch a cold'; note the particle 에.
examples: It takes an hour to get home
A fixed expression every beginner needs.
How long does it take to get here?
Common question when asking about distance/time.
nuance: 걸리다 is a high-frequency verb with two everyday meanings: time being needed (시간이 걸리다) and catching an illness or getting caught (감기에 걸리다, 경찰에 걸리다). For the 'take time' meaning the subject is the time, so you say 시간이 걸려요, not 시간을 걸려요. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 걸리 + 어 → 걸려요.
mistakes: For catching a cold, use the particle 에 (감기에 걸리다), not 를.

usage: 넘다 = cross over something high like a hill or wall.
넘다 also means a number/time has been exceeded.
examples: Used for amounts exceeding a number.
nuance: 넘다 means to go over or pass beyond a limit — a wall, a mountain, a number, or a time. For physical crossing the object takes 을/를 (산을 넘다), but for exceeding a number the subject takes 이/가 (열 시가 넘었어요). It is a regular consonant-stem verb, so 넘 + 어요 → 넘어요. Compare with the excluded 넘어지다 (to fall over), which is a different verb.
mistakes: Don't mix up 넘다 (go over) with 넘어지다 (fall down/trip) — they look similar but mean opposite-feeling things.

usage: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus, train, or chance.
examples: The most typical use for transport.
I was late because I missed the subway
nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were trying to catch — a bus, a train, or a chance — and it always takes 을/를. Don't confuse it with 보고 싶다 (to miss a person). It's a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요. It often appears with 늦다 (to be late) in everyday excuses.
mistakes: To say you miss a PERSON, use 보고 싶다, not 놓치다 — 놓치다 is only for missing a bus, chance, etc.

usage: 떨어지다 also means a supply is used up.
The cup fell on the floor
examples: Daily use for supplies running out.
My wallet fell on the floor
떨어지다 also means failing a test.
nuance: 떨어지다 is the intransitive 'fall' — something drops by itself (지갑이 떨어졌어요). It has two more everyday meanings beginners meet fast: a supply running out (돈이 떨어졌어요) and failing an exam or interview (시험에 떨어졌어요). It is a regular 지다-type verb, so 떨어지 + 어 → 떨어져요. The excluded 떨어뜨리다 is the transitive 'to drop something'.
mistakes: 떨어지다 means something falls on its own; to say YOU drop something, use 떨어뜨리다.

usage: 오르다 is the go-to verb for prices/numbers rising.
오르다 can mean climbing up too.
examples: Prices have gone up these days
Very common with 물가 (cost of living).
nuance: 오르다 means to rise or go up — prices, temperature, level, or climbing a mountain. It is a 르-irregular verb: before -아/어 the 르 changes and an extra ㄹ appears, giving 올라요 and past 올랐어요 (not 오르어요). For everyday speech about prices rising, Koreans say 값이/물가가 올랐어요. Compare the excluded 올라가다 (to go up / ascend), which is the directional pair.
mistakes: Because it's 르-irregular, the past is 올랐어요, never 오르었어요.

usage: Used when water/things won't come out of a tap, etc.
What time do you come out (leave)?
나오다 also means coming out of a place/leaving.
examples: Said about food being served at a restaurant.
Water isn't coming out of the tap
What time do you get off work (come out)?
nuance: 나오다 is 'come out' — toward the speaker or out of a place. It pairs with 나가다 (to go out, away from the speaker), so direction matters in Korean even when English just says 'come/go out'. Because the stem ends in 오, 오 + 아 contracts to 와, giving 나와요 and past 나왔어요. It is extremely common for food being served, water running, and people leaving work.
mistakes: Use 나오다 when something moves toward you/out to where you are; use 나가다 when it moves away from you.

usage: 넣다 = put something into a container/place.
I put the book in the bag
examples: I put sugar in the coffee
I put my wallet in the bag
nuance: 넣다 means to put something into a place or container, so it needs both the thing (을/를) and the destination (에): 가방에 책을 넣어요. Although the stem ends in ㅎ, verbs with ㅎ are regular (unlike ㅎ adjectives), so it's simply 넣 + 어요 → 넣어요. Its natural opposite is 빼다 (to take out).
mistakes: 넣다 is a regular verb — don't drop the ㅎ; the past is 넣었어요, not 너었어요.

usage: 빼다 is used to ask for an ingredient to be removed.
I took the book out of the bag
examples: Please take the cucumber out of the gimbap
I took my hand out of my pocket
nuance: 빼다 means to take something out or remove it, and in math, to subtract. When ordering food it's the polite way to ask for an ingredient to be left out: 빼 주세요. The source takes 에서 (가방에서 빼다). Since the stem ends in ㅐ, 빼 + 어 just contracts to 빼, so the present is 빼요 and the past is 뺐어요. It is the natural opposite of 넣다.
mistakes: The present is just 빼요 (not 빼어요) because the ㅐ stem absorbs the 어.

usage: 차다 = kick, most often with a ball.
In soccer you kick the ball with your feet
examples: Shall we kick a soccer ball together?
nuance: 차다 most commonly means to kick (a ball), and it takes 을/를 for what you kick. Because the stem ends in ㅏ, 차 + 아 contracts to 차, so the present is 차요 and the past is 찼어요. Note that 차다 is a busy word in Korean — it can also mean 'to be full' or 'to wear (a watch)' — but for a beginner, 'kick' is the core meaning to lock in first.
mistakes: The present is just 차요 (not 차아요) — the ㅏ stem absorbs the 아.

usage: Common apology situation on a crowded subway.
Be careful, don't step on it
examples: Sorry, I stepped on your foot
Said after bumping someone in a crowd.
Please don't step on the flowers
A polite request not to step on something.
nuance: 밟다 means to step on or tread on something, and it takes 을/를. The spelling looks like it might be ㅂ-irregular, but it is actually regular: the ㅂ stays, so it conjugates 밟 + 아요 → 밟아요 (pronounced like 'balba-yo'). It comes up constantly in crowded places like the subway, paired with 미안해요 or 죄송해요.
mistakes: 밟다 is NOT ㅂ-irregular — keep the ㅂ: it's 밟아요, not 발워요.

usage: 다니다 = regularly go to a place like school/work.
Standard way to say where you work.
examples: I work at a big company
I go to the gym these days
nuance: 다니다 means to go to a place regularly — to attend school, commute to a job, or frequent the gym — so it implies repetition, not a one-time trip. The place takes 에 (학교에 다녀요). It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 다니 + 어 → 다녀요. To say where you work or study, 다니다 is more natural than 가다.
mistakes: For 'I work at a company', say 회사에 다녀요 — using 가요 would mean a single trip, not your job.

english: to stop (a vehicle) / to stand up
usage: 세우다 = bring a vehicle to a stop.
examples: The key taxi sentence for getting out.
세우다 also means standing something up.
nuance: 세우다 is the transitive 'stand something up / bring it to a stop' — most usefully, telling a taxi driver to stop: 여기 세워 주세요. It's the causative pair of 서다 (to stand/stop, by itself). Because the stem ends in 우, 우 + 어 contracts to 워, giving 세워요 and past 세웠어요. Beginners should memorize 세워 주세요 as a ready-made phrase for taxis.
mistakes: Use 세우다 to stop a car (cause it to stop); 서다 is when something stops on its own.
